items.stem: "Of course he would be late; he was always late." In a third-person passage, this sentence most likely shows:

items.stem: Explain how focalisation can shape the reader's sympathy.
items.answer: Seeing events through one character's perceptions gives access to their feelings and reasons, which tends to align the reader with them even if their actions are questionable.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel (an original extract written for study).

Margit checked the oven again. Six o'clock. He had said six. The table was set for two, the good glasses out, the candles not yet lit – no point lighting candles for nobody. Of course he would be late; he was always late, and she always forgave him, and that was the arrangement, wasn't it? She lit the candles anyway. Let them burn.

Explain how the choice of narrator affects the reader's response to events.
items.answer: Third-person limited narration using free indirect discourse: phrases such as "no point lighting candles for nobody" and "wasn't it?" blend the narrator's voice with Margit's thoughts, giving intimate access to her resentment.
items.markingKey: Third-person limited narration using free indirect discourse: phrases such as "no point lighting candles for nobody" and "wasn't it?" blend the narrator's voice with Margit's thoughts, giving intimate access to her resentment. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following opening of a novel (an original extract written for study).

The summer the river went quiet, Papa started sleeping in the afternoons. Mama said he was tired from the factory, but the factory had stopped making its noise too, so I did not see how. I counted the boats that didn't come. Fourteen on Monday. On Tuesday I stopped counting, because Mama said numbers were for people with jobs.

Identify the narrative point of view in this extract and explain its effect on the reader.
items.answer: First-person child narrator, probably retrospective ("The summer the river went quiet"). The narrator does not understand what the reader infers – that Papa has lost his job – so the naive voice creates dramatic irony and pathos.
items.markingKey: First-person child narrator, probably retrospective ("The summer the river went quiet"). The narrator does not understand what the reader infers – that Papa has lost his job – so the naive voice creates dramatic irony and pathos. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The choice of narrative voice is the most important decision a novelist makes."
items.answer: Narrative voice is arguably foundational because it filters every other element, though its effects depend on how it interacts with them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: voice controls access, sympathy and irony; the same plot changes completely with a different narrator. Arguments against: structure, characterisation and setting also shape meaning; voice works with other elements. Supported judgement: Narrative voice is arguably foundational because it filters every other element, though its effects depend on how it interacts with them.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "indirect characterisation"?

A narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt because of bias, ignorance, self-deception or deceit
A flashback: a narrative return to events earlier than the main story
The attribution of human feelings to nature or the weather, often to reflect a character's mood
items.answer: Character revealed through speech, actions, thoughts, appearance and others' reactions, for the reader to infer
items.markingKey: A. "indirect characterisation" is character revealed through speech, actions, thoughts, appearance and others' reactions, for the reader to infer.

In the town of San Isidro, where the wind came down from the mountains every afternoon at four, nobody owned a clock that told the right time. Read the following extract from a play (an original extract written for study).

[A kitchen, late evening. A single bulb. AMIRA, 17, sits with a university acceptance letter. Her father, KARIM, enters, still in his work jacket.]
KARIM: You're up late.
AMIRA: (folding the letter quickly) Reading.
KARIM: Reading what?
AMIRA: Nothing. Just – school.
KARIM: (picks up her empty mug, rinses it, his back to her) Your mother would have read everything you wrote. Every word.
[Pause. AMIRA slides the letter under the fruit bowl.]

How does the writer characterise the people in this extract?
items.answer: Karim is characterised through work clothes and a domestic gesture – tired, caring, grieving; Amira through evasion.
items.markingKey: Karim is characterised through work clothes and a domestic gesture – tired, caring, grieving; Amira through evasion. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel (an original extract written for study).

Afterwards, everyone would say that the signs had been there. The dog that refused to go into the barn. The letter Tomás never opened, propped against the salt jar for a week. But that morning was ordinary: eggs, rain, the radio murmuring about prices in the capital. Nobody looks for signs on an ordinary morning.

Analyse how symbolism contributes to the meaning of the extract.
items.answer: The unopened letter and the dog refusing to enter the barn work as ominous symbols.

items.stem:
Read the following opening of a novel (an original extract written for study).

The summer the river went quiet, Papa started sleeping in the afternoons. Mama said he was tired from the factory, but the factory had stopped making its noise too, so I did not see how. I counted the boats that didn't come. Fourteen on Monday. On Tuesday I stopped counting, because Mama said numbers were for people with jobs.

Explain the effect of the narrative's treatment of time and sequence in this extract.
items.answer: The retrospective opening frames the summer as significant; the short time markers (Monday, Tuesday) compress days and build towards the revealing final remark.
items.markingKey: The retrospective opening frames the summer as significant; the short time markers (Monday, Tuesday) compress days and build towards the revealing final remark. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel (an original extract written for study).

Margit checked the oven again. Six o'clock. He had said six. The table was set for two, the good glasses out, the candles not yet lit – no point lighting candles for nobody. Of course he would be late; he was always late, and she always forgave him, and that was the arrangement, wasn't it? She lit the candles anyway. Let them burn.

To what extent does the narrative perspective control the reader's sympathies in this extract?
items.answer: Third-person limited narration using free indirect discourse: phrases such as "no point lighting candles for nobody" and "wasn't it?" blend the narrator's voice with Margit's thoughts, giving intimate access to her resentment.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short novel translated from Spanish (an original passage written for study).

The señora paid Rosa on Fridays, in cash, counting each note aloud as if Rosa might not know her numbers. Rosa had taught three of the señora's children to read. She said nothing. She folded the money twice and put it in her shoe, where the señora's eyes did not follow.

Evaluate the effectiveness of the indirect characterisation in this extract.
items.answer: Rosa is characterised by silence and dignity; the señora by unconscious condescension.

items.stem: "Setting is the key to understanding character in prose fiction." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Setting is often central, but its importance lies in its interaction with character rather than determining it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: social setting shapes characters' choices; place often reflects inner states. Arguments against: characters may resist their setting; voice and action also reveal character.
